title: VTE prevention, DVT and PE
blurb: Prevent hospital-acquired VTE under NG89, care safely for people in anti-embolism stockings, and follow the NG158 Wells pathways for suspected DVT and PE.
question: Mr Byrne, 72, admitted with pneumonia, has peripheral arterial disease. A healthcare assistant is about to fit anti-embolism stockings. Three days later his calf is swollen and tender. What should the nurse do about the stockings, and how is the suspected DVT investigated?

teach.body: Formally: venous thromboembolism (VTE) covers deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE). NICE NG89 covers reducing the risk of hospital-acquired VTE; NG158 covers diagnosis and treatment. In plain English: immobility, illness and surgery make clots likely; most can be prevented by assessing risk, mobilising, keeping people hydrated and using the right prophylaxis, and suspected clots must be investigated quickly.

items.label: Assess VTE and bleeding risk
items.sub: as soon as possible, or by first consultant review

items.label: Assess in ED if not yet admitted

teach.h: Anti-embolism stockings: do NOT offer if (NG89 1.3.1)
head: Contraindication
Why
rows: Suspected or proven peripheral arterial disease
Fragile skin, dermatitis, gangrene, recent graft
Severe leg oedema or allergy to material
teach.caption: If arterial disease is suspected, seek expert opinion before fitting stockings (1.3.4).

items: Measure the legs and fit the correct size; trained staff fit them and show the person how to use them.
Wear day and night until mobility is no longer significantly reduced.
Remove daily for hygiene and to inspect the skin; 2 or 3 times a day if mobility is very reduced, skin is poor or there is sensory loss, especially heels and bony prominences.
Stop if there is marking, blistering, discolouration, pain or discomfort; offer intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) if suitable.

teach.body: For acutely ill medical patients whose VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk, offer pharmacological prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days, with LMWH first-line (fondaparinux if LMWH is contraindicated). Start as soon as possible and within 14 hours of the decision to admit. Alongside this: encourage mobilisation as soon as possible and do not let people become dehydrated unless clinically indicated.

teach.note: Explain that IPC reduces the risk of DVT and may improve survival, but will not help stroke recovery.

children.label: Proximal leg vein ultrasound
children.sub: result within 4 h; if not, D-dimer + interim anticoagulation

teach.caption: PE Wells: likely if more than 4 points (CTPA immediately if possible); 4 or fewer, D-dimer first. Interim therapeutic anticoagulation while results are awaited.

head: DVT Wells (1 point each)
PE Wells
rows: Bedridden 3+ days or surgery within 12 weeks
Calf swelling 3 cm+ vs other side

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mr Byrne on a medical ward
teach.body: Staff nurse Aisha stops the stockings being fitted: Mr Byrne has peripheral arterial disease, a contraindication. His risk assessment supports LMWH, which is started within 14 hours of admission, and he is encouraged to mobilise and drink. On day 3 his calf is swollen and tender: DVT Wells 2 (recently bedridden 3+ days, localised tenderness). Aisha escalates; DVT is 'likely', so a proximal leg vein ultrasound is requested, with interim anticoagulation if it cannot be done within 4 hours.

teach.text: Stockings are NOT a harmless default: they are contraindicated in peripheral arterial disease, neuropathy, fragile skin and acute stroke. Also, DVT 'likely' starts at 2 Wells points, but PE 'likely' needs MORE than 4 points. Confirmed proximal DVT or PE: apixaban or rivaroxaban first-line for at least 3 months (NG158 1.3).

items: Assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission (or first consultant review); reassess at consultant review and if condition changes.
Medical patients: LMWH for at least 7 days if VTE risk outweighs bleeding; start within 14 hours of the decision to admit.
Stockings: measure, fit, remove daily to check skin; never with PAD, neuropathy, fragile skin or acute stroke.
Acute stroke: IPC within 3 days for immobile patients, for 30 days or until mobile.
DVT Wells 2+: ultrasound within 4 h; PE Wells over 4: CTPA; treat with apixaban/rivaroxaban for at least 3 months.

summary: You can now assess and reassess VTE risk, choose and care for mechanical and drug prophylaxis safely (including the acute stroke exception), and follow the NG158 Wells pathways for suspected DVT and PE through to first-line treatment.

A.q: When should an adult medical patient be assessed for VTE and bleeding risk under NG89?
A.why: NG89 1.1.2: assess all medical patients as soon as possible after admission or by the first consultant review (or in ED if not admitted within 12 hours).

whyNot.0: 72 hours is too late for the first assessment.
whyNot.1: Assessment at discharge misses the admission risk period.
whyNot.2: Assessment is for all patients on admission, not triggered by immobility.

A.q: Which patient should NOT be offered anti-embolism stockings?
options: A man after elective hip surgery
A man with pneumonia and poor mobility
A.why: NG89 1.3.1: do not offer anti-embolism stockings to people with peripheral neuropathy or other causes of sensory impairment.

whyNot.1: Stockings may be appropriate after hip surgery if there are no contraindications.
whyNot.2: Reduced mobility is an indication rather than a contraindication.
whyNot.3: Abdominal surgery is not a contraindication.

A.q: For how long should an acutely ill medical patient with high VTE risk usually receive pharmacological prophylaxis?
A.why: NG89 1.4.6: offer pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days to acutely ill medical patients whose VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk.

whyNot.1: 28 days is extended prophylaxis after some cancer surgery, not routine medical prophylaxis.
whyNot.2: 3 months is the minimum treatment duration for confirmed VTE.

B.q: A man in anti-embolism stockings has significantly reduced mobility after a fall. How often should his skin be inspected?
B.why: NG89 1.3.7: remove stockings daily, and inspect the skin 2 or 3 times a day if mobility is significantly reduced, skin integrity is poor or there is sensory loss, particularly over heels and bony prominences.

whyNot.0: Weekly inspection risks missing pressure damage.
whyNot.1: Daily removal is the minimum; higher-risk people need more frequent checks.
whyNot.3: Hourly inspection is not the NG89 standard.

B.q: A man with an acute stroke is immobile. What does NG89 recommend for mechanical VTE prophylaxis?
B.why: NG89 1.4.2–1.4.3: do not offer anti-embolism stockings in acute stroke; consider IPC for immobile patients, started within 3 days.

whyNot.1: Stockings are not offered for VTE prophylaxis after acute stroke.
whyNot.2: Stockings of any length are not offered after acute stroke.
whyNot.3: IPC should be considered for immobile stroke patients.

B.q: A woman with suspected DVT has a Wells score of 1. What is the next step under NG158?
options: Proximal leg vein ultrasound in 4 hours
Start warfarin and review in a week
D-dimer with a result in 4 hours
B.why: NG158 1.1.8: DVT unlikely (1 point or less): offer a D-dimer test with the result within 4 hours, or interim anticoagulation if it cannot be obtained in time.

whyNot.0: Ultrasound first is for a likely score (2 or more), or after a positive D-dimer.
whyNot.2: Warfarin without investigation is not the pathway.

C.q: Mrs Lowe, 68, in stockings after surgery, has blistering and discolouration over her heel. What should the nurse do?
options: Reapply a smaller size of stocking
Pad the heel and keep the stockings on
Stop the stockings and consider IPC
Remove them for 1 hour then refit
C.why: NG89 1.3.9: stop stockings if there is marking, blistering or discolouration, particularly over heels and bony prominences, or pain; offer IPC as an alternative if suitable.

whyNot.0: A tighter stocking would worsen the damage.
whyNot.1: Continuing stockings over blistered skin is unsafe.
whyNot.3: A short break does not address the skin damage.

C.q: Mr Ito, 55, has a suspected PE. His PE Wells score is 6. CTPA cannot be done for 5 hours. What does NG158 advise?
options: D-dimer first, then CTPA if positive
Leg ultrasound instead of a CTPA
C.why: NG158 1.1.18: PE likely (more than 4 points): CTPA immediately if possible; if it cannot be done immediately, offer interim therapeutic anticoagulation.

whyNot.0: A D-dimer first is for PE 'unlikely' scores of 4 or less.
whyNot.1: A likely PE needs prompt imaging and anticoagulation, not discharge.
whyNot.2: Leg ultrasound does not replace imaging for suspected PE here.

C.q: A man has a confirmed proximal DVT and no contraindications. Which treatment does NG158 recommend first-line, and for how long at minimum?
C.why: NG158 1.3.5 and 1.3.8: offer apixaban or rivaroxaban for confirmed proximal DVT or PE, and anticoagulation for at least 3 months.

whyNot.0: Aspirin is not treatment for DVT.
whyNot.1: 7 days of LMWH is prophylaxis duration, not treatment.
whyNot.3: Warfarin is not first-line, and 6 weeks is shorter than recommended.

reteach.title: Prevent, protect, probe
reteach.question: How can you hold the whole VTE lesson in three words?

blocks.body: Prevent: assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission, reassess when things change, mobilise and hydrate, give LMWH when risk outweighs bleeding. Protect: if stockings are used, check they are safe for that person (no arterial disease, neuropathy, fragile skin or acute stroke), measure, fit and inspect skin daily. Probe: when a leg swells or someone becomes breathless, use the Wells score to choose ultrasound, D-dimer or CTPA, and do not wait to anticoagulate if results are delayed.

blocks.text: DVT Wells 'likely' = 2 or more. PE Wells 'likely' = more than 4. Don't swap them.

explain.body: Assess VTE and bleeding risk as soon as possible after admission or by first consultant review; reassess at consultant review or if the condition changes. Start prophylaxis within 14 hours of the decision to admit.

test.q: When should VTE and bleeding risk be reassessed under NG89?
options: Every 7 days, on a fixed cycle
test.why: NG89 1.1.8: reassess VTE and bleeding risk at the point of consultant review or if the clinical condition changes.

whyNot.1: NG89 does not set a fixed weekly cycle.
whyNot.2: Handover is not the NG89 reassessment point.
whyNot.3: Waiting until discharge misses changes during the stay.

explain.body: Not for PAD, bypass grafts, neuropathy or sensory loss, fragile skin, severe oedema, allergy or acute stroke. Measure, fit, show how to use, wear day and night, remove daily.

test.q: What does NG89 advise before fitting stockings if arterial disease is suspected?
options: Fit them and check pulses daily
Use a size larger than measured
test.why: NG89 1.3.4: if arterial disease is suspected, seek expert opinion before fitting anti-embolism stockings.

whyNot.0: Length does not remove the arterial risk.
whyNot.3: Stockings must be the measured size.

explain.body: Wells 2+ (likely): proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours, D-dimer if negative. Wells 1 or less: D-dimer within 4 hours; ultrasound if positive. Interim anticoagulation if results delayed.

test.q: A man scores 3 on the DVT Wells score. What is the first investigation?
test.why: NG158 1.1.3: DVT likely (2 or more): offer a proximal leg vein ultrasound with the result within 4 hours if possible.

whyNot.0: D-dimer first is for the unlikely group.
whyNot.2: Venography is not the NG158 first test.

explain.body: PE Wells over 4: CTPA immediately (or interim anticoagulation). 4 or less: D-dimer first. Confirmed DVT or PE: apixaban or rivaroxaban, for at least 3 months.

test.q: A woman's PE Wells score is 3. What is the next step under NG158?
test.why: NG158: PE unlikely (4 points or less): offer a D-dimer test, with imaging if positive.

whyNot.1: Immediate CTPA is for a likely score (more than 4).
whyNot.2: V/Q is an alternative to CTPA for specific groups, not the first step here.
whyNot.3: Echo is not the NG158 first test.
